title: Eight Navy Sailors Attempted Suicide During High-Stress USS Abraham Lincoln Deployment, Letter Reveals
snippet: Internal Navy records reveal eight suicide attempts occurred within the USS Abraham Lincoln strike group during a prolonged, combat-heavy deployment in the Middle East.
content:
Editor’s Note: This story deals with mental health and self-harm. If you or someone you know is in crisis, support is available. In the U.S., call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

Eight U.S. Navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during a grueling deployment that featured continuous combat operations in the Middle East, according to an internal military document.

The figure was disclosed by Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao in a letter to Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), who had inquired about crew morale and mental health conditions. The tally encompasses sailors aboard the aircraft carrier itself, as well as those assigned to the air wing, staff, and escort destroyers across the 6,000- to 7,000-person strike group. Cao noted that no sailors lost their lives to suicide during the deployment.

Impact of Record Sea Time and Combat Stress

While the overall rate of self-harm attempts roughly mirrors the broader active-duty Navy average for 2024, defense officials acknowledged that eight attempts within a single carrier strike group is exceptionally high. Standard carrier deployments typically report only one or two attempts in a given year.

The USS Abraham Lincoln spent months deployed in the Middle East without standard port visits, maintaining a demanding operational tempo against regional threats. Navy personnel aboard the vessel previously described exhausting conditions compounded by daily quality-of-life issues, including frequent shutoffs of fresh water and working toilets.

The letter also confirmed specific crisis events at sea. In March, crew members intervened to stop a sailor from jumping overboard. In another incident in August, a sailor went overboard but was quickly pulled from the water and treated by shipboard medical personnel.

Political Backlash and Support Resources

In a statement addressing the findings, Sen. Gillibrand sharply criticized federal leadership, arguing that official dismissals of reported crew distress ignored deteriorating shipboard environments. She called the lack of adequate support for service members performing high-stress combat missions unacceptable.

Addressing care availability, Cao stated the strike group deployed with dedicated support staff, including five chaplains, a psychologist, a clinical social worker, behavioral health technicians, an integrated prevention counselor, and a facility dog. Navy representatives emphasized that mental health resources remain readily available and that every service member's well-being is taken seriously.

The Lincoln departed the Middle East in August and made a brief port stop in Thailand before heading toward its homeport in San Diego.
